# Wind direction during the steam-train pass

## Which shot this is

The shot in question runs from roughly **27.3 s to 33.8 s** of the clip. It is a
high, elevated view over the San Francisco waterfront: the Embarcadero belt-line
railroad runs horizontally across the middle of the frame, a big arched pier-head
building stands at the left, pier sheds and the bay (with a ferry on it) fill the
top of the frame, and freight cars and low sheds fill the foreground. A steam
locomotive works its way **from left to right** along the belt line, throwing up a
tall, dense white plume that is by far the brightest thing in the frame. This is
the only shot in the clip in which a heavily smoking steam train crosses the
frame left-to-right, so it is unambiguously the one being asked about.

## The answer

**The wind is blowing from left to right across the camera frame.** It comes
*from* the left-hand side of the picture and blows *towards* the right-hand side —
that is, broadly the same direction the train itself is travelling, so it is a
following wind (a tail wind) rather than a head wind.

Two further points about it:

- **It is a light wind.** The smoke is carried to the right at only a fraction of
  the locomotive's own ground speed — the train outruns the air it is moving
  through. That is why the plume still leans backwards even though the air is
  moving forwards (see the next section).
- **It is not blowing towards or away from the camera to any noticeable degree.**
  The plume rises and streams off to the right and over the pier sheds behind the
  tracks; nothing is carried down towards the viewer, and the smoke is not
  flattened onto the ground. It thins out and disperses quickly, which is also
  what you would expect of a light breeze acting on a mostly-steam exhaust.

## Why the plume nevertheless *looks* like it leans left

This is the one thing that is easy to misread, so it is worth stating explicitly.
Freeze any single frame — 30.9 s, 31.7 s, 32.5 s, 33.3 s all show it — and the
white column clearly **tilts back towards the left** as it rises: the foot of the
column sits over the locomotive's stack (around x = 265 px in the 360-px-wide
frame at 31.7 s) while the top of the column is some 20 px further left.

That backward lean is **not** evidence of a right-to-left wind. It is simply how a
plume from a *moving* chimney looks: each puff is abandoned at the spot where it
was emitted while the engine drives on, so the column always trails behind the
locomotive. The question of wind is settled by what a puff does *after* the train
has left it behind — and those abandoned puffs move to the **right**, never to the
left.

## Evidence

I measured this rather than eyeballing it. The shot was decoded to its native
29.97 fps frames, the film was stabilised (the print has noticeable gate weave,
up to ±7 px of per-frame jitter, removed by matching two static building patches
against a reference frame), a per-pixel median background image was built, and
the smoke was isolated as everything significantly brighter than that background.

1. **Abandoned smoke drifts right.** I cross-correlated the smoke field between
   frames 0.27 s apart using a window lying **strictly behind (to the left of) the
   locomotive** — 25 to 85 px behind the stack and well above the track — so the
   window holds only already-emitted smoke and no fresh emission. Over 133 usable
   frame pairs the best-fit horizontal shift is **positive (rightwards)**: median
   +1 px and mean +1.6 px per 0.27 s, i.e. roughly **+4 to +5 px/s to the right**.
   The distribution is plainly skewed positive (28 pairs at +1, 16 at +2, 9 at +3
   versus 9 at −1, 6 at −2, 3 at −3). Running the identical correlation on a
   static textured part of the frame as a control returns a distribution centred
   on **0 px**, so this is not a registration artefact.

2. **The whole smoke structure migrates rightward — nothing is left behind on the
   left.** Rendering the stabilised, background-subtracted smoke masks with fixed
   vertical reference gridlines every 20 px and stepping through 29.8 → 32.8 s,
   the trailing (left-hand) edge of the cloud advances from x ≈ 185 px to
   x ≈ 225 px and the cloud's centre from x ≈ 211 px to x ≈ 254 px. Every part of
   the plume moves to the right; no part of it moves left.

3. **An x–t (slit-scan) diagram shows the same thing.** Collapsing the smoke band
   above the tracks to one row per frame and stacking frames downwards in time
   produces a single bright streak running consistently **down and to the right**,
   with no leftward-running structure anywhere in the shot.

4. **The train outruns the wind, which is why the plume still trails.** Tracking
   the plume's foot (the stack position) gives a locomotive ground speed of about
   **+12 to +15 px/s to the right**, appreciably faster than the smoke's drift.
   With the engine moving right faster than the air, the airflow *relative to the
   locomotive* is still from ahead, so the column bends backwards (leftwards)
   even though the air itself is moving rightwards. The observed lean (about 20 px
   of backward offset over 40 px of rise) is consistent with a modest following
   wind and inconsistent with an opposing one, which would lean the column over
   considerably harder.

5. **Independent confirmation from the immediately preceding shot (≈21.9–27.2 s).**
   That shot looks *along* the Embarcadero from a first-floor height, and the
   locomotive in it is essentially **stationary** — comparing 22.2, 23.4, 24.6,
   25.8 and 27.0 s, the engine holds the same position and size in frame. A
   stationary smoke source makes it a clean wind gauge, with no self-motion to
   confuse things. The same stabilise-subtract-correlate procedure on its large
   hanging smoke cloud gives a very tight result: **+2.7 px/s, again rightwards**,
   with a per-pair histogram of only 0, +1, +2 and +3 px and **not a single
   negative value**. The cloud's brightness centroid marches from x ≈ 210 px to
   x ≈ 250–270 px across the shot, and to the naked eye the smoke visibly piles up
   towards the upper right of that frame.

## A note on compass bearings

Everything above is stated relative to the camera frame, which is what the
footage actually supports. I looked at whether the wind could be pinned to a
compass direction as well, and I do not think it can be done reliably here. The
elevated shot appears to look roughly perpendicular to the waterfront, out over
the piers towards the bay, which would make frame-right roughly south-easterly
and imply a north-westerly wind — the ordinary prevailing San Francisco wind.
But the camera bearings are not consistent between shots (the island visible in
the bay sits on the right of frame at 15 s and on the left at 50 s, so the
viewpoints differ), and reading the preceding Embarcadero shot the same way gives
a bearing that contradicts it. There are no flags, wind vanes or readable ship
plumes anywhere in the clip to settle it. So the compass direction should be
treated as an unverified guess, whereas the frame-relative finding is directly
measured and firm: **the wind blows from the left of the frame towards the right,
carrying the smoke in the same direction the train is travelling, at well under
the train's own speed.**

# Answer

**The wind is blowing from left to right across the camera frame, in the same direction the steam train is travelling, and a little slower than the train.** The smoke is being carried along with (behind and slightly trailing) the locomotive rather than being blown back against it.

## Where in the video

The steam-train shot runs from about 0:27.5 to 0:33.7. The camera looks from a high vantage point across a waterfront: pier sheds and a crane in the middle distance, the bay beyond. The locomotive runs along the tracks in front of the pier sheds, moving left to right at roughly 12 px/s in the 360x240 frame, and puts out a thick white plume.

## What the smoke does

1. The plume rises as a tall, compact, nearly vertical column directly above the locomotive. Its upper part leans only slightly toward the upper-left (i.e. slightly behind the engine). It never streams out in a long low trail behind the train.
2. Tracked against the fixed background (piers, crane, buildings), the smoke moves to the RIGHT the whole time, at every height:
   - fresh smoke at the stack moves right at the train's speed (about 12 px/s);
   - older smoke high above the track (30-60 px above the base) still moves right at roughly 5-10 px/s, i.e. about half to three quarters of the train's speed, while rising slowly at only about 5-10 px/s.
   - A space-time (x versus t) plot of the smoke for each height band shows every smoke streak slanting to the right at close to the train's slope; there are no vertical (stationary-over-the-ground) streaks, so no smoke is being left behind in still air, and nothing drifts to the left.
3. Because the high smoke rises slowly, the smoke at the top of the column is several seconds old. In that time the engine has moved 60-120 px, yet that old smoke sits only about 15-25 px behind the engine. It can only be there if the air itself is carrying it rightward at nearly the train's speed. In still air the plume would trail far behind to the left; with a right-to-left (head) wind it would trail even farther. Neither happens.

## Conclusion

- Wind direction in the frame: left to right (blowing toward the right-hand side of the frame, the direction the train is heading). For the train this is a tailwind.
- Wind speed: somewhat less than the train's speed, which is why the plume lags a little and leans slightly back toward the upper-left instead of standing perfectly vertical or leaning forward.
- The slight backward lean of the plume top is therefore NOT evidence of a right-to-left wind; it is just the difference between the train's speed and the (slower) left-to-right wind. Vertically the smoke rises; no toward/away-from-camera component can be separated from that rise.
